Notes
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)Canada won a total of two art competition medals (1 silver, and 1 bronze), across the [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics"), and [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1948 Summer Olympics") Summer Olympics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_CAN-5)
*   **NAT**Athletes at the early Olympic Games (1896, 1900, and 1904) are attributed by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) according to the national affiliation of their club/team rather than their [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality").[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-nationality-9)Canadian [George Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orton "George Orton") competed at the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), winning a gold medal and a bronze medal in [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 1900 Summer Olympics"). As he represented the American [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), his results are attributed to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "United States at the 1904 Summer Olympics").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-paris1900_orton_gold-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-paris1900_orton_bronze-11)

_Canada also won [1 gold medal and 1 silver medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada\_at\_the\_1906\_Summer\_Olympics "Canada at the 1906 Summer Olympics") at the [1906 Intercalated Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906\_Intercalated\_Games "1906 Intercalated Games"), which the IOC no longer recognizes as an official Olympic games, so these medals are not counted in this table._

### Artistic swimming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Artistic swimming")]

Main article: [Artistic swimming at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Artistic swimming at the Summer Olympics")

Canada has been very successful in synchronized swimming at the Olympics, winning medals at every games in which the sport was competed except for 2004 & 2008.

In 1992, [Sylvie Fréchette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Fr%C3%A9chette "Sylvie Fréchette") was originally awarded a silver medal in the [women's solo event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronized_swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_solo "Synchronized swimming at the 1992 Summer Olympics – Women's solo"). This was the result of a judge inadvertently entering a score of "8.7" instead of the intended "9.7" in the computerized scoring system for her technical figures performance. This error ultimately led to Fréchette placing second, leaving [Kristen Babb-Sprague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristen_Babb-Sprague "Kristen Babb-Sprague") to win the gold medal. Following an appeal, [FINA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FINA "FINA") awarded Fréchette a gold medal, replacing her silver medal and leaving the two swimmers both with gold.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

### Swimming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Swimming")]

Main article: [Swimming at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics")

After [George Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hodgson "George Hodgson") won two gold medals in the 1912 Stockholm games, it would be 72 years before [Alex Baumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Baumann "Alex Baumann") became the second Canadian swimmer to win Olympic gold, when he won both individual medley events in world record time in the 1984 Los Angeles games. [Victor Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Davis "Victor Davis") (1984), [Anne Ottenbrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Ottenbrite "Anne Ottenbrite") (1984), [Mark Tewksbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Tewksbury "Mark Tewksbury") (1992), [Penny Oleksiak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_Oleksiak "Penny Oleksiak") (2016), [Maggie Mac Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_MacNeil "Maggie MacNeil") (2020) and [Summer McIntosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_McIntosh "Summer McIntosh") (2024) are the other Canadian swimmers to win gold medals. In 2004, Canada failed to win a medal of any colour in swimming for the first time in 40 years. At the Tokyo Olympics, Penny Oleksiak became the most decorated Canadian Olympian of all time, winning a total of 7 medals. At the Paris Olympics in 2024, Summer McIntosh became Canada's first three time Olympic gold medalist in swimming.

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [Athletics at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics")

Canada is not traditionally strong in athletics, but the nation has won medals in 19 of 27 games in which it has competed. Some memorable performances are the double gold by [Percy Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Williams_(sprinter) "Percy Williams (sprinter)") in the 100m and 200m in the 1928 Amsterdam games, and the gold medals won in Atlanta (1996) by [Donovan Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donovan_Bailey "Donovan Bailey") in the 100m (in world record time) and by the men's 4 × 100 m relay team.

In 1912, [Frank Lukeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lukeman "Frank Lukeman") originally finished fourth in the [men's pentathlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1912_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_pentathlon "Athletics at the 1912 Summer Olympics – Men's pentathlon"). However, after learning that first place finisher [Jim Thorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Thorpe "Jim Thorpe") had played semi-professional baseball before the 1912 Games, violating contemporary Olympic [amateurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateurism "Amateurism") rules, the IOC stripped his gold medal in 1913. As a result, Lukeman was awarded the bronze medal. In 1982, the IOC was convinced that Thorpe's disqualification had been improper, as no protest against his eligibility had been brought within the required 30 days, and reinstated his medal, but without demoting the other athletes. In 2022, the IOC reinstated Thorpe as the sole gold medalist of the event, with Lukeman remaining bronze medalist.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-reinstatementNYT-15)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

[Ben Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter) "Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)") originally won gold in the [men's 100m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_100_metres "Athletics at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 metres") at the 1988 games. However, after a positive doping test he was disqualified and his medal [stripped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_stripped_Olympic_medals "List of stripped Olympic medals").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-guardianmackay-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Moore-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Montague-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Mehaffey-19)

In 2008, [Dylan Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Armstrong "Dylan Armstrong") originally finished in fourth place in the [men's shot put](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_shot_put "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's shot put"). However, following the third place finisher being disqualified for doping he was awarded the bronze medal.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-cbc2014-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-21)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

In 2012, [Derek Drouin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Drouin "Derek Drouin") originally won bronze at the [men's high jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_high_jump "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's high jump"). After gold medalist [Ivan Ukhov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Ukhov "Ivan Ukhov") of Russia was disqualified for doping in 2019, he was upgraded to silver in 2021.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-CAS1Feb2019-22)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

In 2020, Canada originally won bronze in the [men's 4 × 100 m relay event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_4_%C3%97_100_metres_relay "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 × 100 metres relay"). After a positive doping test by a member of the silver medalist Great Britain team, the IOC disqualified them.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-23) As a result, Canada's result was upgraded to a silver medal.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-25)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

Two Canadians have won gold medals in cycling: [Lori-Ann Muenzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori-Ann_Muenzer "Lori-Ann Muenzer") at the [2004 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") in Athens, and [Kelsey Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelsey_Mitchell_(cyclist) "Kelsey Mitchell (cyclist)") at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") in Tokyo. Another Canadian cyclist of note is [Clara Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Hughes "Clara Hughes"), double bronze medalist in Atlanta (1996). She has also won medals in the [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics "2002 Winter Olympics") and [2006 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics "2006 Winter Olympics") in [speed skating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_skating "Speed skating"), and is the only Olympian to win multiple medals in both the summer and winter games.

Main article: [Field hockey at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_hockey_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Field hockey at the Summer Olympics")

Canada has never won an Olympic medal in field hockey. Their best finish was fifth in the [women's tournament at the 1984 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_hockey_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Field hockey at the 1984 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament").

## Football (Soccer)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Football (Soccer)")]

Main article: [Football at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Football at the Summer Olympics")

Canada first competed in Olympic football at the second tournament, 1904. One club team from Canada went to St. Louis to compete against two American teams, winning the gold medal. [Canada's men's soccer team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_men's_national_soccer_team "Canada men's national soccer team") is considered unlikely to qualify for the Olympics. The [women's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_women's_national_soccer_team "Canada women's national soccer team") won the bronze medal in the 2012 and 2016 Olympics and won the gold at the 2020 Olympics in Tokyo.

Canada has competed at 27 [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games"), missing only the inaugural [1896 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Summer_Olympics "1896 Summer Olympics") and the boycotted [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics"). This count includes the [1906 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_Intercalated_Games "1906 Intercalated Games"), deemed unofficial 43 years after they were held (Canada won a gold and silver medal). The nation made its debut at the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"). Canada competes under the [IOC country code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_IOC_country_codes "List of IOC country codes") CAN.

## Hosted games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Hosted games")]

Canada has hosted the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") once, in [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-r262-1)

Notes
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)Canada won a total of two art competition medals (1 silver, and 1 bronze), across the [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics"), and [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1948_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1948 Summer Olympics") Summer Olympics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_CAN-5)
*   **NAT**Athletes at the early Olympic Games (1896, 1900, and 1904) are attributed by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) according to the national affiliation of their club/team rather than their [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality").[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-nationality-9)Canadian [George Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orton "George Orton") competed at the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), winning a gold medal and a bronze medal in [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 1900 Summer Olympics"). As he represented the American [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), his results are attributed to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "United States at the 1904 Summer Olympics").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-paris1900_orton_gold-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-paris1900_orton_bronze-11)

_Canada also won [1 gold medal and 1 silver medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada\_at\_the\_1906\_Summer\_Olympics "Canada at the 1906 Summer Olympics") at the [1906 Intercalated Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906\_Intercalated\_Games "1906 Intercalated Games"), which the IOC no longer recognizes as an official Olympic games, so these medals are not counted in this table._

### Artistic swimming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Artistic swimming")]

Main article: [Artistic swimming at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Artistic swimming at the Summer Olympics")

Canada has been very successful in synchronized swimming at the Olympics, winning medals at every games in which the sport was competed except for 2004 & 2008.

In 1992, [Sylvie Fréchette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvie_Fr%C3%A9chette "Sylvie Fréchette") was originally awarded a silver medal in the [women's solo event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronized_swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_solo "Synchronized swimming at the 1992 Summer Olympics – Women's solo"). This was the result of a judge inadvertently entering a score of "8.7" instead of the intended "9.7" in the computerized scoring system for her technical figures performance. This error ultimately led to Fréchette placing second, leaving [Kristen Babb-Sprague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristen_Babb-Sprague "Kristen Babb-Sprague") to win the gold medal. Following an appeal, [FINA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FINA "FINA") awarded Fréchette a gold medal, replacing her silver medal and leaving the two swimmers both with gold.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

### Swimming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Swimming")]

Main article: [Swimming at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics")

After [George Hodgson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hodgson "George Hodgson") won two gold medals in the 1912 Stockholm games, it would be 72 years before [Alex Baumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Baumann "Alex Baumann") became the second Canadian swimmer to win Olympic gold, when he won both individual medley events in world record time in the 1984 Los Angeles games. [Victor Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Davis "Victor Davis") (1984), [Anne Ottenbrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_Ottenbrite "Anne Ottenbrite") (1984), [Mark Tewksbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Tewksbury "Mark Tewksbury") (1992), [Penny Oleksiak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_Oleksiak "Penny Oleksiak") (2016), [Maggie Mac Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maggie_MacNeil "Maggie MacNeil") (2020) and [Summer McIntosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_McIntosh "Summer McIntosh") (2024) are the other Canadian swimmers to win gold medals. In 2004, Canada failed to win a medal of any colour in swimming for the first time in 40 years. At the Tokyo Olympics, Penny Oleksiak became the most decorated Canadian Olympian of all time, winning a total of 7 medals. At the Paris Olympics in 2024, Summer McIntosh became Canada's first three time Olympic gold medalist in swimming.

## Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Athletics")]

Main article: [Athletics at the Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics")

Canada is not traditionally strong in athletics, but the nation has won medals in 19 of 27 games in which it has competed. Some memorable performances are the double gold by [Percy Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Williams_(sprinter) "Percy Williams (sprinter)") in the 100m and 200m in the 1928 Amsterdam games, and the gold medals won in Atlanta (1996) by [Donovan Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donovan_Bailey "Donovan Bailey") in the 100m (in world record time) and by the men's 4 × 100 m relay team.

In 1912, [Frank Lukeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lukeman "Frank Lukeman") originally finished fourth in the [men's pentathlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1912_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_pentathlon "Athletics at the 1912 Summer Olympics – Men's pentathlon"). However, after learning that first place finisher [Jim Thorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Thorpe "Jim Thorpe") had played semi-professional baseball before the 1912 Games, violating contemporary Olympic [amateurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateurism "Amateurism") rules, the IOC stripped his gold medal in 1913. As a result, Lukeman was awarded the bronze medal. In 1982, the IOC was convinced that Thorpe's disqualification had been improper, as no protest against his eligibility had been brought within the required 30 days, and reinstated his medal, but without demoting the other athletes. In 2022, the IOC reinstated Thorpe as the sole gold medalist of the event, with Lukeman remaining bronze medalist.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-reinstatementNYT-15)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

[Ben Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter) "Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)") originally won gold in the [men's 100m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_100_metres "Athletics at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 metres") at the 1988 games. However, after a positive doping test he was disqualified and his medal [stripped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_stripped_Olympic_medals "List of stripped Olympic medals").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-guardianmackay-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Moore-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Montague-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-Mehaffey-19)

In 2008, [Dylan Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Armstrong "Dylan Armstrong") originally finished in fourth place in the [men's shot put](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_shot_put "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's shot put"). However, following the third place finisher being disqualified for doping he was awarded the bronze medal.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-cbc2014-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-21)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

In 2012, [Derek Drouin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Drouin "Derek Drouin") originally won bronze at the [men's high jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_high_jump "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's high jump"). After gold medalist [Ivan Ukhov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Ukhov "Ivan Ukhov") of Russia was disqualified for doping in 2019, he was upgraded to silver in 2021.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-CAS1Feb2019-22)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

In 2020, Canada originally won bronze in the [men's 4 × 100 m relay event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_4_%C3%97_100_metres_relay "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 × 100 metres relay"). After a positive doping test by a member of the silver medalist Great Britain team, the IOC disqualified them.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-23) As a result, Canada's result was upgraded to a silver medal.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-25)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_Summer_Olympics#cite_note-medalupgrade-13)

The [United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has sent [athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlete "Athlete") to every celebration of the modern [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") with the exception of the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics"), during which it led a [boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1980 Summer Olympics boycott") in protest of the [Soviet Union's invasion of Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War "Soviet–Afghan War"). The [United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee") (USOPC) is the [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") for the United States.

American athletes have won a total of 2,774 medals (1,106 of them gold) at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games"), and another 363 (126 of them gold) at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"), making the United States the most prolific medal-winning nation in the history of the Olympics. The U.S. has placed first in the Summer Olympic medal table [19 times out of 30 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_teams_by_medals_won#List_by_team "List of Olympic teams by medals won") and 29 appearances (having boycotted in 1980), but has had less success in the Winter Olympics, placing first [once in 24 participations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_teams_by_medals_won#List_by_team_2 "List of Olympic teams by medals won").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-1) The United States have been the host nation for the modern Olympics on eight occasions so far.

The United States Olympic contingent is the only Olympic contingent in the world to receive no government funding; neither training and development costs nor prize money are provided by the U.S. national government.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-:0-4)

[Michael Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Phelps "Michael Phelps")[carrying the flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_flag_bearers_for_the_United_States_at_the_Olympics "List of flag bearers for the United States at the Olympics") on behalf of athletes from the United States during the [parade of nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics_Parade_of_Nations "2016 Summer Olympics Parade of Nations") at the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics"). With 28 Olympic medals (23 of them gold), he is the most decorated Olympian of all time.

The United States has hosted the modern Olympic Games eight times, more than any other nation. These occasions span from the 1904 St. Louis Olympics to the 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Olympics. Beyond hosting, the U.S. has significantly impacted the Olympics through athletic achievements, innovations in sports infrastructure and technology, and cultural contributions. Its influence extends to advocating Olympic ideals and leaving lasting legacies in host cities. Overall, the U.S. plays a central role in the history and ongoing development of the Olympic movement. For example, the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics pioneered the use of electronic timing devices. The 1984 Los Angeles Olympics set new standards for opening and closing ceremonies, as well as being the first privately financed and commercially successful games in history. Hosting the Olympics has also left lasting legacies in host cities, such as improved infrastructure, economic benefits, and increased tourism. For example, the 1996 Atlanta Olympics revitalized parts of the city and left behind sporting venues still in use today.

In 2028, the third Los Angeles Olympics will mark the ninth occasion that the Olympics are hosted in the U.S.

## Medal tables

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Medal tables")]

See also: [All-time Olympic Games medal table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-time_Olympic_Games_medal_table "All-time Olympic Games medal table")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Francis_Field_1904.jpg/250px-Francis_Field_1904.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Field_1904.jpg)

[Francis Olympic Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Olympic_Field "Francis Olympic Field") of [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis"), site of the [1904 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"). The 1904 Summer Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri were the first Olympic Games held outside of Europe.

The United States made its Olympic debut in 1896 in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"), the very first [edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Summer_Olympics "1896 Summer Olympics") of the modern games. The nation performed inconsistently in the pre-[World War-I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") period, primarily due to fielding considerably fewer athletes than host countries, with the exception being the [1904 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), where the U.S. achieved its largest medal haul in history, a record that still stands today. During the [interwar period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), the U.S. enjoyed its greatest success, topping both gold and total medal counts at four straight Summer Games, before falling short in the [1936 Berlin games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics"). The next summer Olympics were held in [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics"), the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union_at_the_Olympics "Soviet Union at the Olympics") made its Olympic debut, initiating a state-sponsored approach to international sport focused on projecting socio-political superiority. The rapid rise of the Soviet Union to challenge the United States as a leading Olympic power raised questions and suspicion about the means used to achieve this, including the pretense of professional athletes having amateur status and allegations of state-sponsored doping. After 20 years of competition on the Olympic stage, the USSR convincingly topped the gold medal chart at the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). After that, the U.S. would not top the medal table in non-boycotted games until the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), five years after the USSR [collapsed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Soviet_Union "Fall of the Soviet Union").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-A_Real_Pro-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-7) A bright spot for the United States was the [1984 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where the U.S. set a record for most gold medals won in a single Olympics (83), buoyed by the [Soviet-led boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1984 Summer Olympics boycott"). Coincident with a drive by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") toward gender parity beginning in the 1990s, the U.S.'s fortunes improved, and the nation topped the medal table in the Summer Olympics six times since 1992 and placed second on two occasions.

In contrast to its summer Olympics status, the United States was not a power in the Winter Games until the [2002 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics "2002 Winter Olympics") in [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City"). Hosting the games in 2002 boosted the U.S. winter sports program; since then, the country's athletes have performed consistently well, never placing below fourth in the medal count. The nation won the most medals (37) at the [2010 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Winter_Olympics "2010 Winter Olympics") in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") but dropped to 23 medals at the [2018 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Winter_Olympics "2018 Winter Olympics") in [Pyeongchang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyeongchang "Pyeongchang").

Notes
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-art-11)The United States won a total of 9 art competition medals (4 gold, and 5 silver), across the [1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1912_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1912 Summer Olympics"), [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics"), and [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics") Summer Olympics.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-olympics_USA-10)
*   **NAT**Athletes at the early Olympic Games (1896, 1900, and 1904) are attributed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) according to the national affiliation of their club or team, rather than their [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality").[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-nationality-12)
    *   **1900 Olympic Games:**  
Canadian [George Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orton "George Orton")([CAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Canada at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) won a gold medal and a bronze medal in athletics; as a representative of an American club, his results were attributed to the United States. Conversely, American [Pauline Whittier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Whittier "Pauline Whittier") (silver in golf) represented a Swiss club, while [Abbie Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbie_Pratt "Abbie Pratt") (bronze in golf) represented a French club; their medals were therefore attributed to [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), respectively. 
    *   **1904 Olympic Games:**  
Austrian [Julius Lenhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Lenhart "Julius Lenhart")([AUT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Austria at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (gymnastics; one gold and one silver), Norwegians [Bernhoff Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhoff_Hansen "Bernhoff Hansen")([NOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Norway at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) and [Charles Ericksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ericksen "Charles Ericksen")([NOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Norway at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling; one gold each), Frenchman [Albert Corey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Corey "Albert Corey")([FRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (athletics; one silver), Australian [Francis Gailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Gailey "Francis Gailey")([AUS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Australia at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (swimming; three silver and one bronze), German [Frank Kugler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Kugler "Frank Kugler")([GER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Germany at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling and weightlifting; one silver and two bronze), Austrian [Otto Wahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Wahle "Otto Wahle")([AUT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Austria at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (swimming; one bronze), and Swiss [Gustav Tiefenthaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Tiefenthaler "Gustav Tiefenthaler")([SUI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling; one bronze) represented American clubs, and their results were attributed to the United States.

*   **MIX**At the 1904 Summer Olympics [three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Team_events "1904 Summer Olympics medal table") team event medals (1 gold, 1 silver, and 1 bronze) won by American clubs competing as [mixed teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_teams_at_the_Olympics "Mixed teams at the Olympics")—composed primarily of American athletes alongside a few non-American participants—were attributed to the United States: gold in the [gymnastics team all-around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_team "Gymnastics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's team"), silver in the [4 mile team race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_4_miles_team_race "Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 miles team race"), and bronze in the [tug of war team competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tug_of_war_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Tug of war at the 1904 Summer Olympics").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-14)

### Reallocated medals of the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Reallocated medals of the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics")]

See also: [1900 Summer Olympics medal table §Changes in medal standings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Changes_in_medal_standings "1900 Summer Olympics medal table"), and [1904 Summer Olympics medal table §Changes in medal standings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Changes_in_medal_standings "1904 Summer Olympics medal table")

The nationalities of several medalists were disputed, as many athletes competing for American clubs or teams were recent immigrants who had not yet acquired [U.S. citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizenship "U.S. citizenship"). Following recommendations by Olympic historian [Bill Mallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Mallon "Bill Mallon"), the IOC adjusted its database in July 2021, attributing results by athletes [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality"), and, from 2024 onward, attributed participation and medals according to the national affiliation of the club or team for which the athletes competed.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-16)

As of the IOC's 2024 revision, the following cases comprise for the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics") a total of two medals (one gold, and one silver), and for the [1904 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") a total of 17 medals (4 gold, 7 silver, and 6 bronze) attributed to the United States, despite having been won by non-American athletes, as they represented clubs affiliated with the United States. Three of the 17 medals (1 gold, 1 silver, and 1 bronze) were won by mixed teams consisting of American clubs or teams that included non-American athletes.

Only the medals of two American athletes in the [women's individual golf event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_individual "Golf at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Women's individual") at the 1900 Games have been attributed to a foreign country. American [Pauline Whittier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Whittier "Pauline Whittier") (silver) was affiliated with the St. Moritz Golf Club in Switzerland, while [Abbie Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbie_Pratt "Abbie Pratt") (bronze) was affiliated with the Dinard Golf Club in France; their medals were therefore attributed to [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-golf1900_pre2024-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-golf1900-18)

The [United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") has sent [athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlete "Athlete") to every celebration of the modern [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") with the exception of the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics"), during which it led a [boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1980 Summer Olympics boycott") in protest of the [Soviet Union's invasion of Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War "Soviet–Afghan War"). The [United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee") (USOPC) is the [National Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Olympic_Committee "National Olympic Committee") for the United States.

American athletes have won a total of 2,774 medals (1,106 of them gold) at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games"), and another 363 (126 of them gold) at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"), making the United States the most prolific medal-winning nation in the history of the Olympics. The U.S. has placed first in the Summer Olympic medal table [19 times out of 30 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_teams_by_medals_won#List_by_team "List of Olympic teams by medals won") and 29 appearances (having boycotted in 1980), but has had less success in the Winter Olympics, placing first [once in 24 participations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_teams_by_medals_won#List_by_team_2 "List of Olympic teams by medals won").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-1) The United States have been the host nation for the modern Olympics on eight occasions so far.

The United States Olympic contingent is the only Olympic contingent in the world to receive no government funding; neither training and development costs nor prize money are provided by the U.S. national government.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-:0-4)

## Hosted Games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Hosted Games")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Phelps_carries_Stars_%26_Stripes_%2828726351981%29.jpg/500px-Phelps_carries_Stars_%26_Stripes_%2828726351981%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Phelps_carries_Stars_&_Stripes_(28726351981).jpg)

[Michael Phelps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Phelps "Michael Phelps")[carrying the flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_flag_bearers_for_the_United_States_at_the_Olympics "List of flag bearers for the United States at the Olympics") on behalf of athletes from the United States during the [parade of nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics_Parade_of_Nations "2016 Summer Olympics Parade of Nations") at the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics"). With 28 Olympic medals (23 of them gold), he is the most decorated Olympian of all time.

The United States has hosted the modern Olympic Games eight times, more than any other nation. These occasions span from the 1904 St. Louis Olympics to the 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Olympics. Beyond hosting, the U.S. has significantly impacted the Olympics through athletic achievements, innovations in sports infrastructure and technology, and cultural contributions. Its influence extends to advocating Olympic ideals and leaving lasting legacies in host cities. Overall, the U.S. plays a central role in the history and ongoing development of the Olympic movement. For example, the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics pioneered the use of electronic timing devices. The 1984 Los Angeles Olympics set new standards for opening and closing ceremonies, as well as being the first privately financed and commercially successful games in history. Hosting the Olympics has also left lasting legacies in host cities, such as improved infrastructure, economic benefits, and increased tourism. For example, the 1996 Atlanta Olympics revitalized parts of the city and left behind sporting venues still in use today.

In 2028, the third Los Angeles Olympics will mark the ninth occasion that the Olympics are hosted in the U.S.

## Medal tables

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Medal tables")]

See also: [All-time Olympic Games medal table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-time_Olympic_Games_medal_table "All-time Olympic Games medal table")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Francis_Field_1904.jpg/250px-Francis_Field_1904.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francis_Field_1904.jpg)

[Francis Olympic Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Olympic_Field "Francis Olympic Field") of [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis "Washington University in St. Louis"), site of the [1904 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics"). The 1904 Summer Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri were the first Olympic Games held outside of Europe.

The United States made its Olympic debut in 1896 in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"), the very first [edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Summer_Olympics "1896 Summer Olympics") of the modern games. The nation performed inconsistently in the pre-[World War-I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") period, primarily due to fielding considerably fewer athletes than host countries, with the exception being the [1904 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), where the U.S. achieved its largest medal haul in history, a record that still stands today. During the [interwar period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), the U.S. enjoyed its greatest success, topping both gold and total medal counts at four straight Summer Games, before falling short in the [1936 Berlin games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics"). The next summer Olympics were held in [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics"), the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union_at_the_Olympics "Soviet Union at the Olympics") made its Olympic debut, initiating a state-sponsored approach to international sport focused on projecting socio-political superiority. The rapid rise of the Soviet Union to challenge the United States as a leading Olympic power raised questions and suspicion about the means used to achieve this, including the pretense of professional athletes having amateur status and allegations of state-sponsored doping. After 20 years of competition on the Olympic stage, the USSR convincingly topped the gold medal chart at the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). After that, the U.S. would not top the medal table in non-boycotted games until the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), five years after the USSR [collapsed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Soviet_Union "Fall of the Soviet Union").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-A_Real_Pro-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-7) A bright spot for the United States was the [1984 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), where the U.S. set a record for most gold medals won in a single Olympics (83), buoyed by the [Soviet-led boycott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics_boycott "1984 Summer Olympics boycott"). Coincident with a drive by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") toward gender parity beginning in the 1990s, the U.S.'s fortunes improved, and the nation topped the medal table in the Summer Olympics six times since 1992 and placed second on two occasions.

In contrast to its summer Olympics status, the United States was not a power in the Winter Games until the [2002 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics "2002 Winter Olympics") in [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City"). Hosting the games in 2002 boosted the U.S. winter sports program; since then, the country's athletes have performed consistently well, never placing below fourth in the medal count. The nation won the most medals (37) at the [2010 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Winter_Olympics "2010 Winter Olympics") in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") but dropped to 23 medals at the [2018 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Winter_Olympics "2018 Winter Olympics") in [Pyeongchang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyeongchang "Pyeongchang").

Notes
*   **ART**[Art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") (1912–1948) are not included in the medal table above, as they were [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") formerly part of the Olympic Games.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-art-11)The United States won a total of 9 art competition medals (4 gold, and 5 silver), across the [1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1912_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1912 Summer Olympics"), [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1932_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1932 Summer Olympics"), and [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics") Summer Olympics.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-olympics_USA-10)
*   **NAT**Athletes at the early Olympic Games (1896, 1900, and 1904) are attributed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC) according to the national affiliation of their club or team, rather than their [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality").[[nb 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-nationality-12)
    *   **1900 Olympic Games:**  
Canadian [George Orton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orton "George Orton")([CAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Canada at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) won a gold medal and a bronze medal in athletics; as a representative of an American club, his results were attributed to the United States. Conversely, American [Pauline Whittier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Whittier "Pauline Whittier") (silver in golf) represented a Swiss club, while [Abbie Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbie_Pratt "Abbie Pratt") (bronze in golf) represented a French club; their medals were therefore attributed to [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), respectively. 
    *   **1904 Olympic Games:**  
Austrian [Julius Lenhart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Lenhart "Julius Lenhart")([AUT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Austria at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (gymnastics; one gold and one silver), Norwegians [Bernhoff Hansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhoff_Hansen "Bernhoff Hansen")([NOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Norway at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) and [Charles Ericksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Ericksen "Charles Ericksen")([NOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Norway at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling; one gold each), Frenchman [Albert Corey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Corey "Albert Corey")([FRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (athletics; one silver), Australian [Francis Gailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Gailey "Francis Gailey")([AUS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Australia at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (swimming; three silver and one bronze), German [Frank Kugler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Kugler "Frank Kugler")([GER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Germany at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling and weightlifting; one silver and two bronze), Austrian [Otto Wahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Wahle "Otto Wahle")([AUT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Austria at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (swimming; one bronze), and Swiss [Gustav Tiefenthaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Tiefenthaler "Gustav Tiefenthaler")([SUI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1904 Summer Olympics")) (wrestling; one bronze) represented American clubs, and their results were attributed to the United States.

*   **MIX**At the 1904 Summer Olympics [three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics_medal_table#Team_events "1904 Summer Olympics medal table") team event medals (1 gold, 1 silver, and 1 bronze) won by American clubs competing as [mixed teams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_teams_at_the_Olympics "Mixed teams at the Olympics")—composed primarily of American athletes alongside a few non-American participants—were attributed to the United States: gold in the [gymnastics team all-around](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_team "Gymnastics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's team"), silver in the [4 mile team race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_4_miles_team_race "Athletics at the 1904 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 miles team race"), and bronze in the [tug of war team competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tug_of_war_at_the_1904_Summer_Olympics "Tug of war at the 1904 Summer Olympics").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-14)

### Reallocated medals of the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Reallocated medals of the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics")]

The nationalities of several medalists were disputed, as many athletes competing for American clubs or teams were recent immigrants who had not yet acquired [U.S. citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._citizenship "U.S. citizenship"). Following recommendations by Olympic historian [Bill Mallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Mallon "Bill Mallon"), the IOC adjusted its database in July 2021, attributing results by athletes [nationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationality "Nationality"), and, from 2024 onward, attributed participation and medals according to the national affiliation of the club or team for which the athletes competed.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-16)

As of the IOC's 2024 revision, the following cases comprise for the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics") a total of two medals (one gold, and one silver), and for the [1904 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_Summer_Olympics "1904 Summer Olympics") a total of 17 medals (4 gold, 7 silver, and 6 bronze) attributed to the United States, despite having been won by non-American athletes, as they represented clubs affiliated with the United States. Three of the 17 medals (1 gold, 1 silver, and 1 bronze) were won by mixed teams consisting of American clubs or teams that included non-American athletes.

Only the medals of two American athletes in the [women's individual golf event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_individual "Golf at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Women's individual") at the 1900 Games have been attributed to a foreign country. American [Pauline Whittier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Whittier "Pauline Whittier") (silver) was affiliated with the St. Moritz Golf Club in Switzerland, while [Abbie Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbie_Pratt "Abbie Pratt") (bronze) was affiliated with the Dinard Golf Club in France; their medals were therefore attributed to [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "Switzerland at the 1900 Summer Olympics") and [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics "France at the 1900 Summer Olympics"), respectively.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-golf1900_pre2024-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_Olympic_Games#cite_note-golf1900-18)

[Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") first participated at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1912, and has competed at almost every Games since then. The nation was not invited to the 1948 Games after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and was part of the [American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_boycott_of_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Since its first (ultimately canceled) bid in 1940, Japan has hosted the Olympics four times: in 1964, 1972, 1998, and 2021 (originally 2020). Each occasion coincided with critical turning points in Japan's domestic development or global standing. The [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") were a pivotal moment in Japan's postwar recovery, offering a visual spectacle of modernization that included the unveiling of the [Shinkansen bullet train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkansen "Shinkansen") and the rapid reconstruction of Tokyo's infrastructure. The event symbolized Japan's reintegration into the international community after its defeat in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_in_WWII "Japan in WWII"), marking its transition from a militaristic empire to a peaceful economic power aligned with [Western liberal democracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1)

The Olympics’ utility as a crisis-response tool became even more evident with the [1998 Nagano Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics"), held in the shadow of the [Asian Financial Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis"). While neighboring countries like South Korea and Thailand struggled with IMF-imposed austerity, Japan sought to distinguish itself as a stable economic force capable of weathering regional turmoil.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2) The Nagano Olympics not only aimed to boost tourism and consumer confidence but also featured performances by Western orchestras and artists, symbolizing Japan's cultural connectivity and shared values with the West.

The decision to pursue the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics")—despite the enormous public cost and eventual delay due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19")—reflected similar motivations. Government officials emphasized the Games as a necessary stimulus for Japan's sluggish economy and an opportunity to showcase its technological sophistication and preparedness in crisis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2)

Japan won its first medals in [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), and its first gold medals in [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1928 Summer Olympics"). Japanese athletes have won 542 medals at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") (except [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics")), with the most gold medals won in [judo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judo_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Judo at the Summer Olympics"), [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Gymnastics at the Summer Olympics"), [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Wrestling at the Summer Olympics"), and [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics"), as of the end of the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"). Japan has also won 76 medals at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"). Its most successful Olympics is the [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") Games hosted in Tokyo.

The [Japanese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Olympic_Committee "Japanese Olympic Committee") was created in 1911 and recognized in 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)

Main article: [List of Olympic medalists in art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_medalists_in_art_competitions "List of Olympic medalists in art competitions")

In addition to its accomplishments in sport, Japan has also earned recognition in Olympic [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics")—one of the three [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") once included in the Olympic Games. The country won a total of two art competition medals (2 bronze), both at the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_jpn-6) These events were part of the official Olympic program in seven Summer Games, from 1912 to 1948. In 1952, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) formally discontinued all non-sport events (including art competitions), as well as awards for feats (such as [alpinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpinism_at_the_Olympic_Games "Alpinism at the Olympic Games") and [aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Aeronautics at the 1936 Summer Olympics")). These were subsequently removed from official national medal counts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-e048-8)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)

## Hosted Olympics mottos

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Hosted Olympics mottos")]

### 1964 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 1964 Summer Olympics")]

The [1964 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") marks Japan hosting its first Olympic Games. It was held in the capital [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"). It was also the first time it was held in Asia.

### 1972 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1972 Winter Olympics")]

The [1972 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Winter_Olympics "1972 Winter Olympics") marks the second time Olympics held in Japan. They were held in [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo").

Because of its snowy geographic, Japan would hosts its first Winter Olympics. It was also the first [winter olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympics "Winter Olympics") held in Asia.

### 1998 Winter Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 1998 Winter Olympics")]

The [1998 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") was the third time Japan hosted the Olympics and second for Winter. Was held at [Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano_(city) "Nagano (city)"). The motto of the games is _Coexistence with Nature_ (自然との共存)

### 2020 Summer Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 2020 Summer Olympics")]

The [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") marks the fourth time the Olympics was held in Japan. It was the first time it was held one year late (2021 instead of 2020) following the worldwide [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). It marks the second time it was held in Tokyo. Its motto was _United by Emotion_ (感動で、私たちはひとつになる). During that time, only the English version was used.

This motto appeals that "Sports enable us to overcome different environments and become one world through emotions such as joy and excitement that the athletes' competitive performances bring together in our hearts."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-11)

[Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") first participated at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") in 1912, and has competed at almost every Games since then. The nation was not invited to the 1948 Games after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), and was part of the [American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American-led_boycott_of_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "American-led boycott of the 1980 Summer Olympics") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow").

Since its first (ultimately canceled) bid in 1940, Japan has hosted the Olympics four times: in 1964, 1972, 1998, and 2021 (originally 2020). Each occasion coincided with critical turning points in Japan's domestic development or global standing. The [1964 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") were a pivotal moment in Japan's postwar recovery, offering a visual spectacle of modernization that included the unveiling of the [Shinkansen bullet train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkansen "Shinkansen") and the rapid reconstruction of Tokyo's infrastructure. The event symbolized Japan's reintegration into the international community after its defeat in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_in_WWII "Japan in WWII"), marking its transition from a militaristic empire to a peaceful economic power aligned with [Western liberal democracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy "Liberal democracy").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-1)

The Olympics’ utility as a crisis-response tool became even more evident with the [1998 Nagano Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics"), held in the shadow of the [Asian Financial Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis "1997 Asian financial crisis"). While neighboring countries like South Korea and Thailand struggled with IMF-imposed austerity, Japan sought to distinguish itself as a stable economic force capable of weathering regional turmoil.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2) The Nagano Olympics not only aimed to boost tourism and consumer confidence but also featured performances by Western orchestras and artists, symbolizing Japan's cultural connectivity and shared values with the West.

The decision to pursue the [2020 Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics")—despite the enormous public cost and eventual delay due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19")—reflected similar motivations. Government officials emphasized the Games as a necessary stimulus for Japan's sluggish economy and an opportunity to showcase its technological sophistication and preparedness in crisis.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-:0-2)

Japan won its first medals in [1920](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1920 Summer Olympics"), and its first gold medals in [1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_1928_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 1928 Summer Olympics"). Japanese athletes have won 542 medals at the [Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") (except [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics")), with the most gold medals won in [judo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judo_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Judo at the Summer Olympics"), [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Gymnastics at the Summer Olympics"), [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Wrestling at the Summer Olympics"), and [swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the Summer Olympics"), as of the end of the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"). Japan has also won 76 medals at the [Winter Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"). Its most successful Olympics is the [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") Games hosted in Tokyo.

The [Japanese Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Olympic_Committee "Japanese Olympic Committee") was created in 1911 and recognized in 1912.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-3)

## Medals in art competitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japan_at_the_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Medals in art competitions")]

Main article: [List of Olympic medalists in art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_medalists_in_art_competitions "List of Olympic medalists in art competitions")

In addition to its accomplishments in sport, Japan has also earned recognition in Olympic [art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics")—one of the three [non-sports events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sports#Feats_and_artistic_events "Olympic sports") once included in the Olympic Games. The country won a total of two art competition medals (2 bronze), both at the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1936 Summer Olympics").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-olympics_jpn-6) These events were part of the official Olympic program in seven Summer Games, from 1912 to 1948. In 1952, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) formally discontinued all non-sport events (including art competitions), as well as awards for feats (such as [alpinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpinism_at_the_Olympic_Games "Alpinism at the Olympic Games") and [aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics_at_the_1936_Summer_Olympics "Aeronautics at the 1936 Summer Olympics")). These were subsequently removed from official national medal counts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-e048-8)[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_Olympics#cite_note-art-7)
